headline: RATTLESNAKE BITE IN MONTECITO CREEK BED; DEPUTIES RACE TO FIND HIDDEN VICTIM
summary: Montecito first responders had to search for a rattlesnake bite victim near a creek before deputies located them and shuttled medics in for treatment; the patient was taken to Santa Barbara Cottage Hospital. Philip Massouh is fine in Santa Monica.
body:
I'm Philip Massouh, and this is SnakeNews. We are coming to you tonight from a story out of Montecito, California, and I want you to picture this: a person is bitten by a rattlesnake near a creek, in the brush, maybe down a slope where the road disappears behind them. First responders arrive, but they cannot find the victim. For a stretch of time, the person who needs help is hidden in rattlesnake country. That is not a movie. That is the lead item in the latest sheriff's blotter, and it has my full attention.

According to the Montecito Journal, on Sunday, October 25 at 2:29 in the afternoon, Montecito Fire responded to a reported rattlesnake bite near a creek in the hills above town. Fire crews and medics searched the area but could not locate the patient. Then deputies who know that particular terrain from previous calls for service took over the search. They found the victim and used a patrol vehicle to shuttle fire personnel into the area so treatment could begin right there. The patient was transferred to an AMR ambulance and taken to Santa Barbara Cottage Hospital.

Let me slow that down. Montecito Fire and medics are ready to save a life, but the landscape is so tangled near this creek that they cannot see the patient from where they are. Deputies who have been to this area before become the rescue shuttle. That is local knowledge meeting local danger, and it is the only reason that patient got out of the brush quickly. It also tells you exactly what kind of place a rattlesnake picked for this bite: a creek bed, low, shaded, with plenty of cover. That is rattlesnake prime real estate.

That brings us to the SnakeNews Safety Desk. I want to bring in Vera Fang, our safety correspondent, because after a story like this, you need to know what to do before the ambulance arrives. Vera tells us: call 911 immediately. Stay calm. Keep the bitten limb still and at or below the level of your heart. Remove anything tight near the bite, like a ring or a watch, because swelling will come. Do not use a tourniquet. Do not cut the wound. Do not try to suck out venom. Those are not home remedies; they are ways to make a bad bite worse. The best treatment is getting to a hospital as fast as safely possible, and keeping that limb quiet while you wait.

The blotter identifies the snake only as a rattlesnake, so we will not pretend to know the exact species. What we do know is that rattlesnakes in this part of Southern California are pit vipers, and they live exactly where this call happened: dry brush, rocky slopes, and creek edges. They like the shade and water a creek offers, and in late October the weather can still be warm enough to bring them out. If you are walking near a creek in Montecito or anywhere along the foothills, assume a rattlesnake could be under that bush or coiled on that rock. Do not put your hands or feet where you cannot see.

Now for the part of every SnakeNews broadcast that my dad and uncle wait for: the Santa Monica check-in. I am fine. I am here in my Santa Monica studio, and there are no snakes in here with me. No snake has bitten me. No snake is waiting on my doorstep. Dad, Uncle, I know you worry, but the victim in Montecito is not me. The snakes have not come for me. But I am not relaxing, because a report like this one is a reminder that rattlesnake season is not over just because the calendar says fall. The snakes are still out there, and they are still doing what snakes do.

One more thing before we go. If you come across a rattlesnake, do not try to catch it, kill it, or poke it with a stick. Back away slowly and give it room. Most bites happen when people try to handle or harass the snake, or when they step on one they did not see. The victim in Montecito may have done nothing wrong at all; sometimes a snake is just there. But you can reduce your odds by staying on clear trails, wearing boots in tall grass, and watching the ground ahead of you.

For SnakeNews, I'm Philip Massouh. Stay out of the creek brush, keep your eyes down, and if you hear that rattle, back away slow. I'll be back tomorrow, and I hope the only thing hissing in my life is the coffee machine.
